nodes.name: Register File
nodes.description:
# Register File Feature Description

The Register File provides the complete memory-mapped register interface for configuring and controlling the SD Host Controller. It implements the standardized register map (starting at offset 000h) that includes command/data transfer registers (SDMA Address, Block Size/Count, Argument, Transfer Mode, Command), status registers (Response, Present State), control registers (Host Control, Power Control, Block Gap Control, Wakeup Control), and the Buffer Data Port for PIO data access.

This feature serves as the primary software interface, allowing the host driver to initiate SD commands, configure transfer parameters, monitor controller state, manage power modes, and handle data movement through either programmed I/O or DMA mechanisms. The register file follows specific initialization requirements, reserved bit handling rules, and supports multiple configuration register types as defined in sections 2.1-2.2 of the specification.

nodes.name: Register Access Types
nodes.description:
# Register Access Types (F_REG_ACCESS_TYPES)

## Purpose and Behavior

This feature defines the various access permission types for SD Host Controller registers, specifying whether registers are Read-Only (RO), Write-Only (WO), Read/Write (RW), or have special behaviors like Read-to-Clear (RWC) or Write-1-to-Clear (W1C). These access types ensure proper register behavior by controlling how software can interact with different register fields—for example, status registers that clear when read, configuration registers that can be freely modified, or capability registers that are read-only and reflect hardware characteristics.

The access type classification is fundamental to the register infrastructure as it prevents unintended register modifications, ensures proper status flag handling, and maintains hardware-software synchronization throughout command execution, data transfer, and interrupt processing operations.

nodes.name: Register Initial Values
nodes.description:
# Register Initial Values Feature Description

This feature defines the power-on reset values for all SD Host Controller registers. Upon hardware reset or power-up, each register in the controller must be initialized to its specified default state as documented in section 2.1.3, ensuring predictable and consistent starting conditions for software initialization. These initial values establish safe defaults (such as disabled interrupts, stopped clocks, and cleared status flags) that allow the host driver to systematically configure the controller before beginning SD card operations.

nodes.name: Reserved Bits Handling
nodes.description:
# Reserved Bits Handling (F_REG_RESERVED_BITS)

## Purpose and Behavior

This feature defines the handling and behavior of reserved bits within the SD Host Controller's register map. According to section 2.1.4, reserved bits must return 0 when read and should be written as 0 by software to ensure forward compatibility with future specification versions that may define functionality for these currently unused bit positions.

The feature ensures proper register access semantics by enforcing that reserved bit fields maintain predictable behavior, preventing software from making assumptions about undefined bits and allowing hardware implementations to potentially use these bits in future revisions without breaking existing driver compatibility.

nodes.name: Command Engine
nodes.description:
# Command Engine Feature Description

The Command Engine is the core control logic responsible for generating and managing SD commands according to the SD specification protocol. It sequences command transmission by formatting command packets with the appropriate command index, argument, CRC, and response type (as configured in the Command Register at offset 00Eh), then transmits them via the CMD line to the SD card while handling response reception and validation.

This engine coordinates with other controller components by monitoring the Present State Register to ensure the CMD line is available, managing command completion interrupts, and supporting advanced features like Auto CMD12/CMD23 for multi-block transfers, ensuring proper command timing and protocol compliance throughout all SD card transactions.

nodes.name: Command Issuance
nodes.description:
# Command Issuance Feature Description

The Command Issuance feature manages the actual transmission of SD commands from the host controller to the SD card. This involves writing command arguments to the Argument 1 Register (offset 008h), configuring transfer parameters in the Transfer Mode Register (offset 00Ch), and triggering command execution through the Command Register (offset 00Eh) which specifies the command index, response type, and command flags (CRC check, index check, data present, etc.).

The feature coordinates with the Present State Register (offset 024h) to ensure the command line is available before issuing commands, and handles the proper sequencing of register writes to generate valid SD protocol command packets on the CMD line. It works as a child component of the Command Engine (F_CMD_ENGINE), implementing the low-level mechanics of command transmission while the parent engine manages higher-level command processing logic.

nodes.name: Command Finalization
nodes.description:
# Command Finalization (F_CMD_FINALIZATION)

## Purpose and Behavior

Command Finalization handles the completion phase of SD command execution within the command engine. This feature manages the post-transmission tasks including response reception (if applicable), response validation, storing response data in the Response Register (offset 010h), and updating the command-related status bits in the Present State Register (offset 024h) to indicate command completion. It also triggers the appropriate Command Complete interrupt and handles any command-related error conditions (timeout, CRC errors, index errors) that may have occurred during the command transaction, ensuring the command engine returns to an idle state ready for the next command.

nodes.name: Command Inhibit
nodes.description:
# Command Inhibit (F_CMD_INHIBIT) Description

Command Inhibit is a status flag in the Present State Register that prevents new SD commands from being issued while the command line (CMD) is busy. This bit is set when a command is being executed on the CMD line and must be checked by software before writing to the Command Register to ensure the previous command has completed. The flag protects against command collisions by blocking new command issuance until the current command transaction finishes and the CMD line returns to idle state, ensuring proper command sequencing in the SD Host Controller's command engine.

nodes.name: Response Handling
nodes.description:
# Response Handling (F_RESPONSE)

The Response Handling feature manages the capture, storage, and retrieval of command responses received from SD cards after command execution. When the SD Host Controller issues a command via the Command Engine, this feature automatically captures the response data from the card (which can be 48-bit short responses or 136-bit long responses) and stores it in the Response Registers (Offset 010h) for software access.

This feature handles different response types (R1, R1b, R2, R3, R6, R7) according to the command specification, validates response timing, and makes the response data available to the host driver through the appropriate register offsets, enabling the software to verify command completion status and retrieve returned data such as card status, OCR values, or CID/CSD information.

nodes.name: Data Transfer
nodes.description:
# Data Transfer Feature Description

The Data Transfer feature manages the movement of data between the SD Host Controller and SD cards during read and write operations. It encompasses multiple transfer mechanisms including programmed I/O (PIO) through the Buffer Data Port Register, Simple DMA (SDMA), and Advanced DMA (ADMA/ADMA2), with control over block sizes, block counts, and buffer management. This feature coordinates with the Transfer Mode Register and Command Register to execute single or multi-block transfers, handles buffer pointer control, supports data transfer suspension/resumption at block boundaries, and manages the data lines' timing and state through the Present State Register to ensure reliable data exchange between host memory and the SD card.

nodes.name: Buffer Data Port
nodes.description:
# Buffer Data Port (F_BUFFER) Description

The Buffer Data Port is a 32-bit register (at offset 020h) that serves as the primary data interface for programmed I/O (PIO) transfers between the host system and the SD Host Controller's internal data buffer. When DMA is not used, the host CPU reads from or writes to this port to transfer data blocks to/from SD cards, with the controller automatically managing the internal buffer pointer advancement after each access. This port provides direct access to the controller's FIFO buffer, enabling block-by-block data transfers under software control as specified in section 1.7 (Buffer Control).

nodes.name: Programmed I/O
nodes.description:
# Programmed I/O (PIO) Feature Description

Programmed I/O is a data transfer method where the host controller CPU directly reads from or writes to the Buffer Data Port Register (offset 020h) to transfer data between system memory and the SD card. Unlike DMA modes, PIO requires software intervention for each data block transfer, with the CPU polling or responding to Buffer Read Ready/Write Ready interrupts to determine when the internal buffer is available for the next transfer operation.

This mode provides a simple, non-DMA alternative for data transfer that doesn't require descriptor tables or dedicated DMA hardware, making it suitable for simple implementations or small data transfers where DMA setup overhead would be inefficient. The host driver must monitor the Present State Register to check buffer availability and manually move data through the Buffer Data Port in response to transfer progress interrupts.

nodes.name: Single DMA
nodes.description:
# Single DMA (SDMA) Feature Description

## Purpose and Behavior

Single DMA (SDMA) is a basic DMA transfer mode that enables direct memory access for data transfers between system memory and the SD Host Controller without CPU intervention. The SDMA engine uses a single system address pointer stored in the SDMA System Address Register (offset 000h) to perform sequential data transfers, automatically incrementing the address as data blocks are transferred. When a 4KB boundary is crossed during multi-block transfers, the controller generates a DMA interrupt, requiring the host driver to reload the next system address into the SDMA register before continuing the transfer.

This mode provides efficient data transfer for SD card operations while maintaining relatively simple implementation compared to Advanced DMA (ADMA), making it suitable for basic host controller designs where memory boundaries can be managed through interrupt-driven address updates.

nodes.name: Advanced DMA 2
nodes.description:
# Advanced DMA 2 (ADMA2) Feature Description

Advanced DMA 2 is an enhanced direct memory access mechanism that enables efficient data transfer between system memory and the SD card without CPU intervention. ADMA2 uses a descriptor table-based architecture where each descriptor specifies memory addresses, data lengths, and transfer attributes, allowing the controller to autonomously execute complex, scatter-gather DMA operations across non-contiguous memory regions.

The feature operates through a state machine that fetches descriptors from system memory, validates address alignment and length requirements, and performs the actual data transfers while generating appropriate interrupts upon completion or errors. This provides superior performance compared to simple SDMA by eliminating the need for CPU intervention during multi-block transfers and supporting more flexible memory layouts through its descriptor-based approach.

nodes.name: ADMA2 Descriptor Table
nodes.description:
# ADMA2 Descriptor Table Description

The ADMA2 Descriptor Table is a memory-resident data structure that defines scatter-gather DMA operations for the SD Host Controller's Advanced DMA (ADMA2) engine. Each descriptor entry in the table specifies attributes (valid, end, interrupt, action type), data length, and physical memory address for a data transfer segment, allowing the controller to autonomously chain multiple non-contiguous memory buffers without CPU intervention. The table is programmed by software and traversed by the ADMA2 state machine, with descriptor formats supporting operations like data transfer (Tran), linking to additional descriptor tables (Link), and no-operation (Nop) entries to enable flexible, high-performance multi-buffer DMA transfers.

nodes.name: ADMA2 State Machine
nodes.description:
# ADMA2 State Machine Description

The ADMA2 State Machine manages the operational states of the Advanced DMA 2 controller during data transfers. It controls the progression through distinct states including Stop, Fetch Descriptor, Change Address, Transfer Data, and potentially error states, orchestrating how the ADMA2 engine reads descriptor entries from the descriptor table and executes the corresponding data transfer operations. This state machine ensures proper sequencing of descriptor fetches, address updates, and actual data movement between system memory and the SD card buffer, handling transitions based on descriptor attributes (Valid, End, Int, Act) and transfer completion conditions.

nodes.name: Block Size and Count
nodes.description:
# Block Size and Count Feature Description

The Block Size and Count feature controls the fundamental parameters for block-oriented data transfers in the SD Host Controller. The Block Size Register (offset 004h) specifies the size of each data block to be transferred (typically 512 bytes for SD cards), while the Block Count Register (offset 006h) determines how many blocks will be transferred in a single transaction. 

Together, these registers enable the controller to manage multi-block read/write operations efficiently by defining the total transfer size (block size × block count) and coordinating with DMA engines, buffer management, and the Auto CMD12 mechanism for automatic command termination after the specified number of blocks have been transferred.

nodes.name: Large Data Transfer Division
nodes.description:
# Large Data Transfer Division (F_LARGE_DATA_DIV)

This feature enables the SD Host Controller to divide large data transfers that exceed the maximum block count (65535 blocks) into multiple smaller transactions. When a transfer requires more blocks than can be specified in the 16-bit Block Count Register, the controller automatically segments the operation into sequential transfers, managing the buffer pointers and block counts across each segment while maintaining data integrity and proper command sequencing throughout the divided transaction.

nodes.name: Auto CMD Mechanism
nodes.description:
# Auto CMD Mechanism (F_AUTO_CMD)

## Purpose and Behavior

The Auto CMD mechanism enables the SD Host Controller to automatically issue CMD12 (STOP_TRANSMISSION) or CMD23 (SET_BLOCK_COUNT) commands without software intervention during multi-block data transfers. This feature eliminates the need for the host driver to explicitly send these commands, reducing interrupt latency and improving transfer efficiency by allowing the controller to seamlessly append the stop/block-count command at the appropriate point in the transfer sequence (after the last data block for CMD12, or before the data transfer for CMD23).

The mechanism is controlled through the Transfer Mode Register and operates in conjunction with the Block Count register, automatically managing the command sequencing and error handling for these auxiliary commands while the main data transfer is in progress.

nodes.name: Auto CMD12
nodes.description:
# Auto CMD12 Feature Description

Auto CMD12 is an automatic command generation feature that enables the SD Host Controller to automatically issue a CMD12 (STOP_TRANSMISSION) command at the end of a multi-block data transfer without software intervention. When enabled via the Transfer Mode Register, the controller automatically sends CMD12 to terminate the data transfer after the programmed number of blocks (specified in Block Count Register) have been transferred, eliminating the need for the host driver to explicitly issue a separate stop command. This streamlines multi-block read/write operations and reduces software overhead while ensuring proper termination of data transfers.

The feature is part of the broader Auto CMD functionality (parent: F_AUTO_CMD) and is controlled through specific bits in the Transfer Mode Register, with its status and any errors reported through dedicated interrupt status bits.

nodes.name: Auto CMD23
nodes.description:
# Auto CMD23 Feature Description

Auto CMD23 enables the SD Host Controller to automatically issue CMD23 (SET_BLOCK_COUNT) before executing a multi-block data transfer command (CMD18/CMD25), eliminating the need for software intervention. This feature programs the block count for the subsequent read or write operation, allowing the controller to handle the entire multi-block transfer sequence autonomously without requiring the host driver to manually send CMD23 first.

When enabled, the controller uses the value in the Block Count Register (Offset 006h) to automatically generate and send CMD23 with the appropriate block count argument before initiating the actual data transfer command, streamlining multi-block operations and reducing software overhead compared to manual CMD23 issuance or the older Auto CMD12 mechanism.

nodes.name: Interrupt System
nodes.description:
# Interrupt System (F_INTERRUPT)

The Interrupt System manages event notification and status reporting within the SD Host Controller by generating hardware interrupts to alert the host processor of command completion, data transfer status, errors, and card state changes. This system consists of interrupt status registers that flag events, interrupt enable registers that control which events generate interrupts, and interrupt signal enable registers that gate the actual interrupt signals to the processor.

The interrupt architecture supports both normal operation events (command complete, transfer complete, buffer ready) and error conditions (timeout, CRC errors, command conflicts), allowing software to efficiently respond to controller events without continuous polling while maintaining precise control over which interrupts are actively monitored and signaled to the system.

nodes.name: Normal Interrupt Status
nodes.description:
# Normal Interrupt Status Feature Description

The Normal Interrupt Status feature provides status flags for successful completion of standard SD Host Controller operations. This register tracks routine events such as command completion, transfer completion, buffer read/write ready states, card insertion/removal, and DMA interrupts, allowing the host driver to monitor and respond to normal operational milestones during SD card transactions.

Each status bit in this register is set by the hardware when the corresponding event occurs and must be cleared by software writing '1' to the bit position. These interrupts work in conjunction with the Normal Interrupt Status Enable and Normal Interrupt Signal Enable registers (as described in section 1.8) to control which events generate actual interrupt signals to the system processor.

nodes.name: Error Interrupt Status
nodes.description:
# Error Interrupt Status Feature Description

The Error Interrupt Status feature provides a dedicated set of status bits that indicate various error conditions occurring during SD Host Controller operations. This feature monitors and reports critical errors such as command timeout, command CRC errors, data timeout, data CRC errors, auto CMD12 errors, ADMA errors, and other protocol violations that occur during command execution or data transfer phases.

When an error condition is detected by the controller hardware, the corresponding error interrupt status bit is set, allowing the host driver to identify the specific failure type and take appropriate recovery actions. This feature works in conjunction with the Error Interrupt Status Enable and Error Interrupt Signal Enable registers (as described in section 1.8 on Interrupt Control Registers) to provide granular control over which error conditions generate interrupts to the system processor.

nodes.name: Interrupt Status Enable
nodes.description:
# Interrupt Status Enable Feature Description

The Interrupt Status Enable feature controls which interrupt status bits are allowed to be set in the Interrupt Status Register. When an interrupt status enable bit is set to 1, the corresponding interrupt event can update its status bit in the Interrupt Status Register; when set to 0, the status bit remains unchanged regardless of the event occurrence. This register acts as a gating mechanism between hardware events and status reporting, working in conjunction with the Interrupt Signal Enable register to provide two-level interrupt control - the Status Enable determines what gets recorded, while the Signal Enable determines what generates actual interrupt signals to the host processor.

This feature is essential for selective interrupt monitoring, allowing software to filter which SD Host Controller events (such as command complete, transfer complete, errors, card insertion/removal, etc.) should be tracked in the status register without necessarily generating interrupt signals.

nodes.name: Interrupt Signal Enable
nodes.description:
# Interrupt Signal Enable Feature Description

The Interrupt Signal Enable feature controls whether interrupt status events are actually propagated as interrupt signals to the system/processor. This register works in conjunction with the Interrupt Status Enable register to provide two-level interrupt masking: while the Status Enable register determines which events are tracked internally, the Signal Enable register determines which of those tracked events generate actual interrupt signals on the host controller's interrupt output line.

Each bit in the Interrupt Signal Enable register corresponds to a specific interrupt source (e.g., command complete, transfer complete, error conditions), and when set to 1, allows that interrupt status to assert the controller's interrupt signal to the CPU, enabling interrupt-driven operation rather than polling-based status checking.

nodes.name: Auto CMD Error Status
nodes.description:
# Auto CMD Error Status Feature Description

The Auto CMD Error Status feature provides detailed error reporting for automatic command operations (Auto CMD12/CMD23) that are issued by the host controller without software intervention. This register captures specific failure conditions such as command timeout, CRC errors, end bit errors, command index errors, and whether the auto command was not executed, allowing software to diagnose why an automatic command sequence failed during multi-block data transfers.

When an error occurs during auto CMD execution, this status register is populated with the specific error type(s) and triggers an interrupt (via the Auto CMD Error interrupt bit in the Error Interrupt Status register), enabling the host driver to take appropriate recovery actions such as issuing manual stop commands or resetting the command/data lines.

nodes.name: Clock System
nodes.description:
# Clock System (F_CLOCK) Description

The Clock System manages the generation and distribution of SDCLK, the clock signal provided to SD cards for synchronous data transfer and command operations. This system controls clock frequency division from a base clock source, enables/disables clock output to the card, and manages internal clock stability through programmable dividers specified in the Clock Control Register (section 2.2.14). The clock system supports dynamic frequency scaling for different speed modes (Default Speed, High Speed, SDR/DDR modes) and includes mechanisms for clock gating during idle periods to reduce power consumption, as detailed in section 1.12 "Controlling SDCLK".

nodes.name: Internal Clock and SDCLK Supply
nodes.description:
# Internal Clock and SDCLK Supply (F_CLK_SUPPLY)

This feature manages the generation and distribution of the internal clock source and the SDCLK signal that drives SD card operations. The internal clock serves as the base timing reference for the host controller, while SDCLK is the divided and gated output clock supplied to the SD card interface, with the host controller providing programmable clock dividers to generate appropriate SDCLK frequencies from the internal clock source. The feature includes clock enable/disable control, stability detection mechanisms, and the ability to gate SDCLK independently from the internal clock to support power management and synchronization requirements during data transfers and command sequences.

nodes.name: Clock Stop Mechanism
nodes.description:
# Clock Stop Mechanism (F_CLK_STOP)

The Clock Stop Mechanism controls the ability to gate or stop the SD clock (SDCLK) to the card when the bus is idle, enabling power savings without requiring a full power-down sequence. This feature allows the host controller to dynamically disable clock output between transactions while maintaining the card's state and connection, then quickly resume clock generation when needed for the next command or data transfer.

The mechanism is typically controlled through the Clock Control Register and works in conjunction with the Present State Register to ensure the clock is only stopped when no command or data transfer is in progress, preventing protocol violations or data corruption.

nodes.name: Clock Frequency Change
nodes.description:
# Clock Frequency Change (F_CLK_FREQ_CHANGE)

## Description

This feature enables dynamic modification of the SD clock (SDCLK) frequency supplied to the SD card by programming the clock divider values in the Clock Control Register. The Host Controller must stop the SDCLK before changing the frequency (by clearing the SD Clock Enable bit), program the new frequency divider, wait for the Internal Clock Stable bit to indicate the new frequency is stable, and then re-enable SDCLK to resume card operations at the new frequency.

Clock frequency changes are essential for supporting different SD card speed modes (initialization at 400 kHz, default speed, high speed, etc.) and for power management optimization by reducing clock frequency during idle periods or low-performance requirements.

nodes.name: Dual Clock Domain
nodes.description:
# Dual Clock Domain Feature Description

The Dual Clock Domain feature enables the SD Host Controller to operate with two independent clock domains: one for the internal host controller logic and another for the SD card interface (SDCLK). This architectural separation allows the host controller's internal operations to run at a different frequency than the clock provided to the SD card, enabling power optimization and flexible clock management.

This feature is critical for implementing dynamic clock scaling, where the SDCLK can be adjusted independently (as described in section 1.12: Controlling SDCLK) without affecting the host controller's internal processing speed, and supports advanced power states (section 1.10) by allowing selective clock gating of different domains while maintaining controller functionality.

nodes.name: Sampling Clock Tuning
nodes.description:
# Sampling Clock Tuning (F_SAMPLING_TUNING)

## Purpose and Behavior

Sampling Clock Tuning is a calibration mechanism that adjusts the timing of the sampling clock used to capture data from the SD card, particularly critical for high-speed modes (SDR50, SDR104, HS200, HS400) where timing margins are tight. The host controller executes a tuning procedure by sending CMD19 (or CMD21 for eMMC) and analyzing the received tuning pattern to determine the optimal sampling point that minimizes bit errors caused by signal propagation delays and clock skew. This feature dynamically compensates for variations in PCB trace lengths, temperature changes, and voltage fluctuations by adjusting internal delay elements or phase-locked loop settings to center the sampling window within the valid data eye, ensuring reliable data capture at higher clock frequencies.

nodes.name: Power Control
nodes.description:
# Power Control (F_POWER) Description

The Power Control feature manages the SD bus voltage supply to the card through the Power Control Register (Offset 029h). It controls both the voltage level selection (3.3V, 3.0V, or 1.8V) and the power enable/disable state of the SD bus, allowing the host controller to power up/down the card and switch voltage levels as required by different card types and operating modes. This feature is essential for card initialization sequences, voltage negotiation during card detection, and power management to reduce system power consumption when the card is idle or not present.

nodes.name: Bus Power and Voltage Select
nodes.description:
# Bus Power and Voltage Select Feature Description

This feature controls the power supply to the SD bus and selects the operating voltage level for SD card communication. It manages the SD Bus Power bit to enable/disable power delivery to the card slot and configures the SD Bus Voltage Select field to set the appropriate voltage level (typically 3.3V, 3.0V, or 1.8V) based on card capabilities and host support. This feature is essential for proper card initialization, voltage negotiation during the card identification process, and enabling low-voltage signaling modes like UHS-I, ensuring the SD card receives stable power at the correct voltage level for reliable operation.

nodes.name: Power States D0-D3
nodes.description:
# Power States D0-D3 Description

The Power States D0-D3 feature defines the operational power modes of the SD Host Controller, following standard PCI/PCIe power management conventions. D0 represents the fully operational state where all controller functions are active, D1/D2 are intermediate low-power states with reduced functionality, and D3 is the deepest sleep state where the controller consumes minimal power and requires reinitialization upon wake. These states enable system-level power management by allowing the host controller to transition between different power consumption levels based on activity requirements, with state transitions typically managed through power control registers and coordinated with the system's power management infrastructure.

nodes.name: 1.8V Signaling Enable
nodes.description:
# 1.8V Signaling Enable Feature Description

The 1.8V Signaling Enable feature controls the voltage level used for signaling between the SD Host Controller and the SD card, switching between 3.3V and 1.8V I/O voltage levels. This feature is essential for enabling high-speed modes like UHS-I (Ultra High Speed) and SDR104/DDR50, which require 1.8V signaling to achieve higher data transfer rates while reducing power consumption.

When enabled, this feature triggers a voltage negotiation sequence with the card and adjusts the host controller's I/O buffers to operate at the lower 1.8V level, typically controlled through the Host Control 2 Register in conjunction with the Power Control Register to ensure proper voltage switching timing and card compatibility.

nodes.name: Bus Width Control
nodes.description:
# Bus Width Control Feature Description

The Bus Width Control feature manages the data bus width configuration between the SD Host Controller and the SD card. This feature allows the host to dynamically switch between 1-bit, 4-bit, and 8-bit data transfer modes by configuring the appropriate bits in the Host Control 1 Register (Offset 028h), enabling optimization of data throughput based on card capabilities and system requirements.

The bus width setting directly affects the parallel data transfer capacity on the DAT lines, where 1-bit mode uses only DAT0, 4-bit mode uses DAT[3:0], and 8-bit mode (for eMMC devices) uses DAT[7:0], with wider bus configurations providing proportionally higher data transfer rates during read and write operations.

nodes.name: Speed Mode Support
nodes.description:
# Speed Mode Support Feature Description

The Speed Mode Support feature enables the SD Host Controller to operate at different clock frequencies and bus signaling speeds to accommodate various SD card types and performance requirements. This feature is primarily controlled through the Host Control 1 Register (Offset 028h) and works in conjunction with the clock control mechanisms (section 1.12) to switch between modes such as Default Speed, High Speed, SDR (Single Data Rate), DDR (Double Data Rate), and UHS (Ultra High Speed) modes. The controller adjusts both the SDCLK frequency and voltage signaling levels to match the negotiated speed mode with the connected SD card, ensuring optimal data transfer rates while maintaining compatibility across different card generations.

nodes.name: Default Speed Mode
nodes.description:
# Default Speed Mode (F_DEFAULT_SPEED)

Default Speed Mode is the baseline SD clock frequency operating mode that supports data transfer rates up to 25 MHz for SD cards and 26 MHz for MMC cards. This mode is controlled through the Host Control 1 Register (Offset 028h) and works in conjunction with the Clock Control Register to configure the SDCLK frequency divider to generate the appropriate clock signal for standard-speed SD/MMC card operations.

As a mandatory P0 feature within the speed_modes group, Default Speed Mode serves as the fundamental speed capability that all SD Host Controllers must support, providing backward compatibility and serving as the initial operating mode during card initialization before potentially switching to higher-speed modes like High Speed or UHS modes.

nodes.name: High Speed Mode
nodes.description:
# High Speed Mode (F_HIGH_SPEED)

High Speed Mode enables the SD Host Controller to operate at clock frequencies up to 50 MHz, providing double the data transfer rate compared to the default speed mode (25 MHz). This mode is activated through the High Speed Enable bit in the Host Control 1 Register (Offset 028h) and requires both the host controller and the SD card to support this capability.

When enabled, the controller adjusts its timing parameters and clock generation to meet the tighter setup and hold time requirements of high-speed signaling, allowing for faster data throughput while maintaining signal integrity on the SD bus interface.

nodes.name: UHS-I SDR50
nodes.description:
# UHS-I SDR50 Feature Description

UHS-I SDR50 (Ultra High Speed-I Single Data Rate 50MHz) is a speed mode that enables SD card data transfers at up to 50 MB/s using a 100 MHz clock with single data rate signaling and 1.8V I/O voltage. This mode requires the SD Host Controller to support programmable clock generation to produce the 100 MHz SDCLK frequency, along with proper voltage switching capabilities and tuning procedures to ensure reliable high-speed data sampling. The controller must implement the UHS-I timing specifications and may require clock tuning (as referenced in section 1.16) to optimize the sampling point for the increased clock frequency compared to legacy modes.

nodes.name: UHS-I SDR104
nodes.description:
# UHS-I SDR104 Feature Description

UHS-I SDR104 is an ultra-high-speed single data rate mode that operates at up to 208 MHz clock frequency, providing a maximum theoretical throughput of 104 MB/s. This mode requires the SD Host Controller to support precise clock tuning capabilities (as defined in section 1.16: Sampling Clock Tuning) to compensate for signal timing variations at high frequencies, and uses 1.8V signaling for reduced power consumption and improved signal integrity. The host controller must be capable of dynamically adjusting the sampling point of the data signal through the tuning procedure to ensure reliable data capture at this elevated speed.

nodes.name: UHS-I DDR50
nodes.description:
# UHS-I DDR50 Feature Description

UHS-I DDR50 is a high-speed transfer mode that enables data transfer at 50 MHz clock frequency using Double Data Rate (DDR) signaling, where data is sampled on both rising and falling clock edges, achieving an effective data rate of 50 MB/s. This mode is selected through the Host Control 1 Register's UHS Mode Select field and requires the SD Host Controller to support 1.8V signaling as specified in the UHS-I (Ultra High Speed Phase I) standard. The DDR50 mode provides a balance between speed and power consumption, offering twice the throughput of SDR25 at the same clock frequency by utilizing both clock edges for data transfer.

nodes.name: Card Detection
nodes.description:
# Card Detection Feature Description

Card Detection monitors the physical presence of an SD card in the slot through hardware mechanisms. The SD Host Controller typically implements this through a mechanical switch in the card slot that changes state when a card is inserted or removed, with the status reflected in the Present State Register (Offset 024h) via the Card Inserted bit. This feature generates interrupts to notify the host software of card insertion/removal events, enabling the system to automatically initiate card initialization sequences or safely handle card removal scenarios.

nodes.name: Write Protection
nodes.description: The Write Protection feature monitors the physical write-protect switch status on SD cards through dedicated pins on the card slot. The SD Host Controller reads this mechanical switch state via the Present State Register and prevents write operations (CMD24, CMD25, etc.) from being issued when the card is write-protected, returning appropriate error status to the host driver. This hardware-level protection ensures data integrity by enforcing read-only access when the card's physical write-protect tab is in the locked position.

nodes.name: Timeout Control
nodes.description:
# Timeout Control (F_TIMEOUT) Description

The Timeout Control feature manages the maximum time period the SD Host Controller will wait for a response from an SD card or for data transfer completion before generating a timeout error. This is implemented through a programmable timeout counter register that defines the timeout value for DAT line busy checks and command response reception, typically using SDCLK cycles as the time base. When the timeout period expires without receiving the expected response or data transfer completion, the controller sets a timeout error status bit in the interrupt status register and halts the current operation, allowing software to detect and handle unresponsive card conditions.

nodes.name: Error Handling
nodes.description:
# Error Handling Feature Description

The Error Handling feature manages the detection, reporting, and recovery from various error conditions that occur during SD Host Controller operations. This includes command timeout errors, CRC errors, data transfer errors, ADMA errors, and auto-CMD errors, which are captured in dedicated error interrupt status registers and can trigger interrupt signals to alert the host driver. The feature provides error status bits that indicate the specific type of failure (e.g., command timeout, data end bit error, current limit error) and enables the controller to halt operations, preserve error state for software diagnosis, and support error recovery mechanisms such as software resets for the command and data lines.

nodes.name: Software Reset
nodes.description:
# Software Reset Feature Description

The Software Reset feature provides a mechanism to reset specific portions or the entire SD Host Controller through software control, typically implemented via bits in the Software Reset Register (part of the Clock Control Register at offset 02Fh). This feature allows the host driver to independently reset the data circuit (DAT line), command circuit (CMD line), or perform a complete controller reset without requiring a hardware power cycle.

Software resets are essential for error recovery scenarios, such as clearing stuck command or data transfer states, recovering from timeout conditions, or reinitializing the controller after detecting protocol violations. The reset operation clears internal state machines, FIFOs, and relevant status flags while preserving critical configuration settings, enabling quick recovery without full reinitialization of the host controller.

nodes.name: Block Gap Control
nodes.description:
# Block Gap Control Feature Description

The Block Gap Control feature enables the SD Host Controller to temporarily halt multi-block data transfers between block boundaries, allowing the host system to perform time-critical operations without aborting the entire transfer. This is controlled through the Block Gap Control Register (Offset 02Ah), which works in conjunction with the Suspend and Resume Mechanism (section 1.6) to pause data transmission after the current block completes, then resume it later from the exact stopping point. This capability is essential for systems that need to service interrupts or handle urgent tasks while maintaining the integrity of large data transfers, as it ensures clean suspension points at block boundaries rather than mid-block interruptions.

nodes.name: Read Wait
nodes.description:
# Read Wait Feature Description

The Read Wait feature enables the SD Host Controller to temporarily pause data transfer from an SDIO card during multi-block read operations by asserting the DAT2 line. This mechanism allows the host to stop the data stream at block boundaries when it needs additional time to process received data or handle higher-priority tasks, without terminating the entire transfer. The feature is controlled through the Block Gap Control Register and is specifically designed for SDIO cards that support the Read Wait protocol, providing flow control during continuous data reads while maintaining the active connection to the card.

nodes.name: Suspend Resume
nodes.description: The Suspend Resume feature enables the SD Host Controller to temporarily halt an ongoing multi-block data transfer at a block boundary and later resume it from the exact point where it was stopped. This is controlled through the Block Gap Control Register (Offset 02Ah), where software can request a suspend by setting the Stop At Block Gap Request bit, causing the controller to pause after completing the current block transfer. The suspended transaction can then be resumed by setting the Continue Request bit, allowing the remaining blocks to be transferred without reissuing the command or losing the transfer context.

nodes.name: Wakeup Control
nodes.description:
# Wakeup Control Feature Description

The Wakeup Control feature enables the SD Host Controller to generate wakeup events that can bring the controller out of low-power states (such as suspend or sleep modes) in response to specific SD card activities. This feature is configured through the Wakeup Control Register (Offset 02Ah) and works in conjunction with the controller's power state management defined in section 1.10.

The feature typically allows the host to wake up on events such as card insertion, card removal, or card interrupt signals, enabling power-efficient operation where the controller can remain in a low-power state until meaningful card activity occurs that requires host attention.

nodes.name: Card Interrupt
nodes.description:
# Card Interrupt Feature Description

The Card Interrupt feature enables the SD Host Controller to detect and handle asynchronous interrupt signals generated by SDIO cards. This interrupt mechanism allows SDIO devices (such as Wi-Fi or Bluetooth modules) to notify the host of events or data availability without requiring the host to continuously poll the card, enabling efficient power management and real-time responsiveness. The feature is controlled through dedicated interrupt control registers that can mask, detect, and signal card interrupt events to the host system, with special handling considerations during multi-block data transfers and when the DAT[1] line is used for interrupt signaling per SDIO specifications.

nodes.name: Capabilities
nodes.description:
# Capabilities Feature Description

The Capabilities feature provides a read-only register interface that exposes the hardware capabilities and supported features of the SD Host Controller to software. This register set allows the host driver to discover what functionalities are implemented in the hardware, such as supported voltage levels, maximum block length, DMA support (SDMA/ADMA), bus widths, clock speeds, timer configurations, and other controller-specific features. By reading these capability registers during initialization, the driver can dynamically configure itself to match the hardware's actual capabilities rather than relying on compile-time assumptions, ensuring proper operation across different SD Host Controller implementations.

nodes.name: Preset Values
nodes.description:
# Preset Values Feature Description

The Preset Values feature provides pre-configured register settings for different SD bus speed modes and driver strengths, allowing the host controller to automatically configure optimal timing parameters (clock divider, driver strength, etc.) when switching between UHS-I and other speed modes. When enabled via the Host Control 2 Register, the controller uses these preset values stored in read-only registers (typically at offsets 060h-06Bh) instead of requiring software to manually program the SDCLK Frequency Select and Driver Strength Select fields. This capability simplifies driver implementation and ensures consistent, validated timing configurations across different operating modes like SDR12, SDR25, SDR50, SDR104, and DDR50.

nodes.name: Host Controller Version
nodes.description: The Host Controller Version feature provides a read-only register that identifies the specific version of the SD Host Controller specification implemented by the hardware. This register allows software drivers to determine the controller's capabilities and feature set by reading a standardized version identifier, enabling proper initialization and compatibility handling across different specification revisions (e.g., SD Host Controller Specification versions 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, etc.). The version information is typically stored in the upper portion of the capabilities register space and is essential for the driver to adapt its behavior to the supported features of that particular specification version.

nodes.name: Force Event
nodes.description:
# Force Event Feature Description

The Force Event feature provides a software mechanism to manually trigger interrupt events in the SD Host Controller for testing and debugging purposes. This is typically implemented through the Force Event Register for Error Interrupt Status, which allows software to artificially generate specific error conditions (such as command timeout, CRC errors, or data end bit errors) without actual hardware events occurring.

This feature is primarily used during controller validation and driver development to verify that interrupt handlers respond correctly to various error scenarios. By writing to specific bits in the Force Event register, developers can simulate error conditions that would otherwise be difficult to reproduce reliably during normal operation.

nodes.name: Multiple Slot Support
nodes.description:
# Multiple Slot Support (F_MULTI_SLOT)

## Purpose and Behavior

Multiple Slot Support enables a single SD Host Controller to manage multiple physical SD card slots simultaneously through a shared register interface. When implemented, the controller uses slot-specific addressing mechanisms to route commands, data transfers, and interrupts to the appropriate card slot, allowing the host system to communicate with multiple SD cards without requiring separate controller instances for each slot.

The feature requires additional logic to multiplex the shared data bus, command lines, and control signals between slots, along with slot selection mechanisms in the register interface to direct operations to the intended card slot. When this feature is marked as NOT_SUPPORTED (as in this case), the controller implements only a single-slot configuration with direct connections between the register set and one physical SD interface.

nodes.name: Shared Bus Control
nodes.description:
# Shared Bus Control Feature Description

Shared Bus Control enables multiple SD slots to share common bus signals (CMD, DAT lines) within an SD Host Controller, allowing a single controller to manage multiple SD cards through slot multiplexing. This feature, part of the multi_slot group, requires coordination mechanisms to arbitrate bus access between slots and ensure only one slot actively communicates on the shared bus at any given time.

When NOT_SUPPORTED (as indicated by the priority), the controller operates in single-slot mode or uses independent buses for each slot, eliminating the need for bus arbitration logic and shared signal routing between multiple card slots.

nodes.name: PME Wakeup
nodes.description:
# PME Wakeup Feature Description

PME (Power Management Event) Wakeup is a power management feature that enables the SD Host Controller to generate a wake signal to bring the system out of a low-power sleep state when specific SD card events occur. When enabled through the Wakeup Control Register (Offset 02Ah), the controller can assert a PME signal in response to card insertion, card removal, or card interrupt events while the host system is in a reduced power state. This feature is particularly important for mobile and embedded systems where the SD interface needs to wake the system processor when an SD card requires attention, allowing the system to remain in low-power states until actual SD activity occurs.
